the black band consortium has an oxygenic phototrophic base, which is responsible for O 2 -rich conditions in the upper part of the consortium.

the band moves by the combined action of photosynthesis and sulfide oxidation, and that the band is a highly dynamic system in which the oxygen and sulfide distributions are controlled by the balance between photosynthesis, sulfide oxidation, respiration and sulfate-reduction, and by the diffusion rates of O _{2}, H _{2} S and H ^{+}.
the black band is a horizontally migrating cyanolichen, that the band is an anaerobic microbial consortium, and that the band is a microbial consortium that is capable of killing corals.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the dynamics of the oxygen and sulfide gradients in the black band microbial consortium, the role of the cyanobacterial photosynthesis and respiration, the sulfide oxidation by Beggiatoa and the role of sulfate-reducing and fermentative bacteria.
understanding the microbial ecology of black band disease and its relationship to coral reef ecology.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the band is a cyanobacterial mat which, in contrast to other mats, is horizontally migrating.
black band disease is caused primarily by a combination of sulfide and O 2 depletion.
black band disease is not a disease in the strict sense, as the band is not pathogenic to the coral.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the band is a cyanobacterial mat which is vertically and horizontally mobile and which is adapted to a sulfide-rich, O 2 -limited environment at its interface with the coral.
oxygen and sulfide are produced and consumed in the band, and that the consortium is capable of migrating horizontally and growing vertically.
the band is a cyanobacterial mat which, because of its high metabolic rate, is able to overgrow coral tissue and kill the coral.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the microbial consortium that causes BBD is not a single organism but a complex consortium of bacteria and fungi that are capable of producing and consuming oxygen and sulfide in a diel rhythm.

the consortium has a similar structure to cyanobacterial mats, and that the consortium's ability to produce O 2 in the presence of sulfide may allow it to persist at the coral surface, despite the anoxia that would otherwise be expected.
oxygen and sulfide dynamics at the band-cora interface are similar to those in many other cyanobacterial mats.
